{{use dmy dates|date=March 2026}}

The '''Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics''' or '''FPOS''' comprise ten standards for the operation of national statistical systems, agreed by the [[United Nations General Assembly|General Assembly of the United Nations]] in 2014 (resolution 68/261). The principles cover professional competence, international cooperation, legal status and independence from political interference. They envision that [[official statistics]] should meet the needs of users across all of society.<ref name=UNECE>{{cite journal|author1=Fiona Willis-Núñez|author2=Małgorzata Cwiek|title=Thirty years on, the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics remain the shared foundation of an informed society|doi=10.3233/SJI-220049|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|volume=38|year=2022|pages=711-723|issue=3|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Origins==
The transition to a market economy from central planning during the [[dissolution of the Soviet Union]] meant countries were developing their statistical capability very quickly.<ref name="Bodin" /> Western European countries also supported standards to assert confidentiality of responses to their surveys.<ref>{{cite web|author=[[John Pullinger]]|url=https://www.civilserviceworld.com/professions/article/uk-civil-service-key-to-global-quality-statistics|publisher=Civil Service World|date=2022-05-12|title=Covid and the war in Ukraine are tragically graphic illustrations of the need for trustworthy data}}</ref> Expectations of professional independence in official statistics, were codified for the first time, drawing on the standards published by [[International Statistical Institute|ISI]] in 1985.<ref name="Seltzer" /><ref>{{cite journal|title=The codification of statistical ethics|author=[[Roger Jowell]]|journal=Journal of Official Statistics|year=1986|volume=2|issue=3|pages=217-253|url=https://www.scb.se/contentassets/ca21efb41fee47d293bbee5bf7be7fb3/the-codification-of-statistical-ethics.pdf}}</ref> There was also an innovation in principle #4 which stipulated that statisticians could comment on erroneous interpretation of official data.<ref name="Bodin" />

Principles to guide the work of official statistics, and maintain their independence from political influence, were developed in the European region in an international working group reporting in 1991. The Fundamental Principles were proposed by the [[Conference of European Statisticians]] (CES) and agreed at the [[UNECE]] in 1992, then by the [[United Nations Statistical Commission|UN Statistical Commission]] (UNSC) at a special session in 1994.<ref name=Seltzer>{{cite report|author=William Seltzer|year=1994|title=Politics and statistics: independence, dependence or interaction?|publisher=[[UNSD]]|series=DESIPA|volume=94/6|type=Working Paper|location=New York|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/statcom/FP-Seltzer.pdf}}</ref> There were no changes to the principles themselves in the wider adoption, just revision to the preamble to change references to the European extent of support.<ref name=Bodin>{{cite proceedings|author=Jean-Louis Bodin|chapter=The Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics: the Breakthrough of a New Era|title=5O YEARS OF THE CONFERENCE OF EUROPEAN STATISTICIANS|pages=63-77|year=2003|publisher=[[UNECE]]|location=Geneva, CH|url=https://unece.org/DAM/stats/publications/50yearsCES.pdf}}</ref>

==Principles==
The principles introduced reflected professional good practice which had not been codified before but principle 4 was regarded as an innovation.<ref name="Bodin" />

==Implementation==
Assessments of the practical adoption of the Fundamental Principles identified a gap between initial aspirations and expectations of stakeholders.<ref name=deV>{{cite journal|author=Willem de Vries|journal=International Statistical Review|title=Are We Measuring Up . . . ? Questions on the Performance of National Statistical Systems|year=1999|volume=67|issue=1|pages=63-77|doi=10.1111/j.1751-5823.1999.tb00381.x}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=[[Tim Holt (statistician)|Tim Holt]]|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|title=The fundamental principles and the impact of using statistics for administrative purposes|volume=15|issue=3-4|pages=203-212|year=1998|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/SJU-1998-153-403|doi=10.3233/SJU-1998-153-403|url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, several countries reported using FPOS as the basis for evaluating whether statistical systems were working as they should, both where these were developing and where they were established.<ref name="deV" /><ref name=Tadeusz>{{cite journal|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|author=Tadeusz Toczynski|year=1998|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/SJU-1998-153-402|doi=10.3233/SJU-1998-153-402|title=The relationship between government and the national statistical institute|pages=191-202|volume=15|issue=3-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This included international governmental bodies, such as the [[IMF]], which republish national data to support international comparisons and may have challenges negotiating user needs and the negotiation of changes to technical standards.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|author1=Heinrich Brüngger|author2=[[Svein Longva]]|year=1998|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/SJU-1998-153-405|doi=10.3233/SJU-1998-153-405|title=International principles governing official statistics at the national level: are they relevant for the statistical work of international organisations as well?|pages=221-235|volume=15|issue=3-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=Carson>{{cite journal|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|author=Carol Carson|year=1998|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3233/SJU-1998-153-404|doi=10.3233/SJU-1998-153-404|title=Fostering the fundamental principles of official statistics|pages=213-220|volume=15|issue=3-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Further attention was extended to propagating the principles in the least developed administrative settings as a condition of entry to global organisations such as the [[OECD]].<ref name="Carson" /> The [[Sustainable Development Goal 17|SDGs]] also mention legislation consistent with FPOS in monitoring goal 17.18<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/metadata/?Goal=17&Target=17.18|publisher=UNSD|title=SDG Indicators Metadata Repository}}</ref> and attention to development of leadership capability was a particular priority in the African region.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Ben Kiregyera|title=Supporting implementation of Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics in the African region|journal=Statistical Journal of the IAOS |date=2017 |volume=33 |issue=4 |page=863-867|doi=10.3233/SJI-170350}}</ref> Although the principles were designed by the national statistical institutes who adopted them, they reflected the good practice in other producers of statistics serving the public good, such as central banks.<ref name="Carson" />

==Consolidation==
Substantial action was taken to introduce or enhance statistical legislation in many countries but tensions about the use of statistics to justify political decisions sustained.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Tim Holt|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A|year=2003|volume=166|issue=3|title=The need for new statistical legislation for the UK|pages=349-367|doi=10.1111/1467-985X.00281}}</ref> When FPOS was ratified by the UN General Assembly in 2014<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/dnss/gp/fundprinciples.aspx|title=Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics (A/RES/68/261 from 29 January 2014)}}</ref> and remitted back to UNSC, they were asked to keep their effectiveness under review.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unece.org/statistics/news/long-journey-fundamental-principles-official-statistics|title=The long journey of the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics|date=2015-01-29|publisher=UNECE}}</ref> The friends of the chair group recommended UNSC focus on promotion of the principles, adherence to them, supporting challenges of misuse, and updating them for new context<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/statcom/doc15/2015-18-FP-E.pdf|title=Report of the Friends of the Chair group on the implementation of the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics|publisher=UNSC|year=2015}}</ref> and that agenda was sustained at the 30th anniversary of adoption in 2022.<ref name="UNECE" />

===Promotion===
The UNECE and CES organised a 30th anniversary recognising the enduring value of FPOS in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://w3.unece.org/fpos30/index.html|title=Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics 30 years 1992-2022|publisher=UNECE}}</ref> Different nations celebrated each of the ten principles and statistical offices produced materials to raise their profile.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unece.org/FPOS30|title=30th Anniversary of the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics|publisher=UNECE}}</ref> The UNECE further developed short text to explain each principle in terms more familiar to a wider range of users to promote them beyond the statistical community.<ref name="UNECE" />

===Adherence===
Implementation guidelines were developed to better explain the practicalities and support wider use following the ratification at the general assembly.<ref>{{cite report|publisher=UNSD|year=2015|title=United Nations Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics:Implementation Guidelines|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/dnss/gp/Implementation_Guidelines_FINAL_without_edit.pdf}}</ref> In 2026 the UNSC established a consultative advisory board to support adherence to the principles by providing advice and developing guidance based on best practices.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/UNSDWebsite/statcom/session_57/documents/BG-3a-FPOS_CAB_Background_document_rev3-E.pdf|publisher=UNSC|title=Consultative Advisory Board on the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics: Terms of Reference and proposed membership}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/fpos/advisory-board.cshtml|title=Consultative Advisory Board on the Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics}}</ref>

===Challenging misuse===
Many countries' statisticians have needed to comment when statistics were misreported by the media<ref name="Tadeusz" /> or misrepresented in public discussion, including by politicians.<ref>{{cite journal|title=How to react when the independence of statisticians and the integrity of statistics are endangered?|author=Jean-Louis Bodin|year=2011|journal=Statistical Journal of the International Association for Official Statistics|doi=10.3233/SJI-2011-0719|volume=27|issue=1-2|pages=59-69}}</ref> In 2020 the [[International Association for Official Statistics]] organised some events on the topics of misuse and the application of principle 4<ref>{{cite web|author=John Pullinger|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/wsd/2020/blog/Misuse-of-statistics-time-to-speak-out.html|date=2020-10-15|title=Misuse of statistics: time to speak out|publisher=UNSD}}</ref> which "protects the right of statistical agencies to speak up when they see errors being made. This means that even when statistics are deliberately or accidentally misused by someone in a powerful position in government, official statisticians can set them straight without fear of reprisal."<ref name="UNECE" />

===Changing context===
The dramatic shift in the importance of data has led to concerns that the principles need updating to apply to AI and other automated uses of data.<ref name="UNECE" /> But the principles are also the basis for national statistical offices making a claim to be at the centre of this transformation, because FPOS represents a coherent and trustworthy framework for data stewardship.<ref>{{cite report|title=Data Stewardship and the Role of National Statistical Offices in the New Data Ecosystem|url=https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/ECECESSTAT20234.pdf|publisher=UNECE|year=2024}}</ref>
